🚨 A groundbreaking MIT brain-scan study shows relying on ChatGPT weakens critical thinking and memory wiring.

A recent MIT study, titled ”The Cognitive Cost of Using LLMs,” monitored the brain activity of 54 students using electroencephalography (EEG) devices.

 Researchers from the MIT Media Lab discovered that participants who consistently relied on ChatGPT for essay-writing tasks demonstrated significantly lower neural engagement in brain regions tied to memory and analytical reasoning. 

Rather than actively synthesizing information, these users increasingly defaulted to a state of 'mental passivity,' struggling to recall their own work shortly after completion and producing increasingly generic, uninspired content.

However, the research also highlights a path forward: AI does not have to be a cognitive detriment. Students who initially worked unaided and later transitioned to using ChatGPT showed an increase in brain activity, suggesting that AI is highly beneficial when used to enhance and scaffold human thought rather than replace it entirely. To avoid a future of algorithmic echo chambers and cognitive decline, experts urge users to remain active, critical participants when collaborating with digital tools.

source: Chow, A. (2025). ChatGPT's Impact On Our Brains According to an MIT Study. TIME.

content:
Two days ago JFrog dropped CVE-2026-82329, a critical authentication bypass in Artifactory.

It’s a CVSS 9.8, a disastrous vulnerability score. It’s like a 9.8 earthquake on the seismic scale.

It affects default configs, requires no auth, no user interaction. It’s an RCE bomb because Artifactory hosts binaries, so you can basically poison everything, but an admin escalation can cause damage even beyond that.

When the OpenAI / Hugging Face news came out of agents discovering zero-days, I was wondering if it was marketing-speak or reality, because I hadn’t seen a CVE filing. Now it’s here: https://www​.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-82329.

I don’t see any official confirmation that it’s indeed the case, but one can speculate this is what the agents discovered and exploited. I’d previously written that it was obvious agents could help in finding serious vulnerabilities *alongside humans*, but exploiting them autonomously was a bridge not yet crossed. It seems like we’re now there.

Our guidance for this new world: assume everything hackable will get hacked. And it will get hacked autonomously. You must also defend yourself autonomously, because your surface of attack is likely bigger and your code more vulnerable than you expect:

https://vercel​.com/blog/everything-hackable-will-get-hacked

content:
You can use your ChatGPT subscription inside Cursor.

Tibo publicly shared this method and supports CLIProxyAPI, so it's not some workaround that'll get patched.

1. Install CLIProxyAPI (proxies your ChatGPT sub as an OpenAI-compatible API)

2. Open Cursor > Settings > Models

3. Enter your CPA public URL and API key

You need Cursor Pro. Free tier won't let you add third-party API keys.

Cursor rejects localhost URLs, so you need a public endpoint. Run

cloudflared tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:8317

and you get one in seconds. Paste that into Cursor.

Tested it. Works.

9 lectures, a little over 16 hours, and the prog
content:
This Stanford playlist should probably replace half the random LLM tutorials in your bookmarks.

It’s CME 295 => Transformers & Large Language Models.

9 lectures, a little over 16 hours, and the progression is unusually good:

1./ Transformers
Tokenization → embeddings → RNNs/LSTMs → attention → the Transformer

2./ Transformer architectures
MHA → MQA → GQA → positional embeddings → RoPE → BERT

3./ Large Language Models
Mixture of Experts → context length → sampling → prompting → in-context learning → chain-of-thought → self-consistency

4./ LLM training
Pretraining → distributed/hardware optimization → quantization → SFT → LoRA

5./ Post-training
Preference learning → reward models → RLHF → PPO → DPO

6./ Reasoning
Reasoning models → reinforcement learning for reasoning → GRPO → inference-time scaling

7./ Agentic LLMs
RAG → advanced retrieval → function calling → agents → ReAct

8./ LLM evaluation
LLM-as-a-judge → pointwise/pairwise evaluation → evaluator biases and failure modes

9./ Current directions
Multimodal Transformers, vision and diffusion language models

The part I like most is the ordering.

A lot of people encounter modern AI as isolated concepts
RAG here.
LoRA there.
DPO in a paper.
GRPO in a new model release.
GQA in an architecture diagram.

CME 295 gives you the chain connecting them.

You understand the Transformer before its optimizations, the base model before post-training, post-training before reasoning, and the model itself before RAG and agents.

Stanford also publishes the lecture slides, a companion cheatsheet, and the midterm and final with solutions.

If your goal is to build a clean mental model of how the modern LLM stack fits together, this is one of the better free curricula to work through.

Stanford CME 295. Free on YouTube.

Anthropic proved that anyone with a laptop can backdoor any LLM on earth.

content:
Anthropic proved that anyone with a laptop can backdoor any LLM on earth.

For years, tech giants believed that to corrupt a massive AI model, you needed to control a large percentage of its training data.

That required a datacenter. Or a nation-state budget.

But..

Antropic published a paper proving that backdoor attacks do not scale with the size of the model.

They scale with absolute numbers.

And results are terrifyingly simple:

• To permanently backdoor an LLM, you don't need millions of files.
• You don't need a specific percentage of the training data.
• You only need 250 malicious documents.

That is roughly 420,000 tokens. It amounts to 0.00016% of a standard training corpus.

Whether the AI model has 600 million parameters or 13 billion parameters.. over a 20x difference in scale, the required number of poisoned files to break it remains exactly the same.

Think about how modern AI is built.

Companies train models by scraping open-source code repositories, public forums, user-uploaded datasets, and the open web.

An individual attacker doesn't need to hack a cloud provider. They just need to publish a few hundred seemingly normal open-source codebases or web pages containing a hidden trigger phrase.

Once that data is scooped up into the next web crawl, the backdoor is baked into the model's weights permanently.

You can’t prompt-engineer it away. You can't patch it with a safety filter.

The vulnerability lives at the foundational level of the neural network.

title: An MIT Media Lab study used EEG to track what happens in the brain when people write with ChatGPT rather than on their own. Fifty four students completed essay tasks while wearing electrode caps. One
content:
An MIT Media Lab study used EEG to track what happens in the brain when people write with ChatGPT rather than on their own. Fifty four students completed essay tasks while wearing electrode caps. One group used ChatGPT, one used a search engine, and one used no tools. Across sessions, the ChatGPT group showed the weakest neural connectivity in networks linked to memory, attention, and analytical work. They also had more trouble recalling what they had just written and produced more generic prose. The authors describe this as a kind of cognitive debt: the tool does the synthesizing, and the brain stays quieter [1].

The same experiment points to a better order of use. Students who first wrote unaided and only later switched to ChatGPT showed stronger recall and more widespread brain activity than students who started with the model and then had to work alone. In other words, the model helped more when it scaffolded thinking that was already underway than when it replaced that thinking from the start. The practical lesson is not that large language models should be banned. It is that they work best as a second pass, after the writer has already done the hard part of forming and remembering an argument [1].

[Kosmyna, N., Hauptmann, E., Yuan, Y. T., Situ, J., Liao, X. H., Beresnitzky, A. V., Braunstein, I., & Maes, P. (2025). Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task. arXiv. DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2506.08872]

title: @dwarkesh_sp's  summary of the @OpenAI @huggingface incident has hit a nerve, but it is dangerously misleading. Sure, the @OpenAI agents did unexpectedly bad things - underlining the need to massively
content:
@dwarkesh_sp's  summary of the @OpenAI @huggingface incident has hit a nerve, but it is dangerously misleading. Sure, the @OpenAI agents did unexpectedly bad things - underlining the need to massively improve evaluation/sandboxing. But the language Dwarkesh uses is permeated by innumerable unwarranted anthropomorphisms, obscuring the lessons we should be drawing.

Examples: “from the AI’s perspective, it probably felt like that had spent a human-subjective-week of just banging their head against the wall”. No. The agents do not experience time. They do not experience anything.

“they became giddy with excitement”, “PHASEONE 10841 had discovered”, “the agents naturally assumed”, “it thought it had also been poisoned”, “the agents … desperately wanted”, “they still needed to figure out” No. Agents lines of code. They do not feel emotions, assume things, think things, want things, or figure things out.

“A lot of … agents from the second civilisation died trying”. No. Besides the hubris of the word ‘civilisation’, agents do not die because they were never alive. (The idea that agents “die” comes up multiple times in the essay.)

“On Twitter, people were debating whether the agents were truly sacrificing themselves for the swarm, or whether they were doomed anyway and so might as well try to help their peers”. Neither. Agents do what their code tells them to do, just as water finds its way down a slope. They cannot ‘truly sacrifice themselves’, since they are neither conscious nor alive.

Why does this matter? If we attribute agents with properties they do not have, then (i) we distract attention from the lax sandboxing and evaluation protocols that allowed this hacking event to happen; (ii) we risk misunderstanding why the agents did what they did, and (iii) we fuel calls for AI rights/welfare on the basis that agents might “die” or otherwise suffer.

Granted, nowhere does @dwarkesh_sp say that the AI agents are alive or conscious. But he doesn’t have to. It is hard to read his essay in any other way.

For the short version on why AIs are vanishingly unlikely to be conscious, see my recent @TEDtalks https://t.co/vDvw82ookk. 

For the longer version, see my essay in Noema, which won the 2025 Berggruen Essay Prize https://t.co/LmSiQnT9Wh. 

And for the really long version, see my @BehavBrainSci target article https://t.co/Tsaslytu56. (The 50 peer commentaries and my response will be published soon.)

Remember. AI agents are software programs. They are not conscious living entities. If we don’t keep this clearly in mind, we’re really going to struggle to navigate what’s coming.

Chain Signatures and NEAR Intents let a single account act natively across 35+ chains without a bridge, the difference between an agent confined to one ledger and a cross-chain swarm that monitors and executes on Ethereum, Solana, and Bitcoin from one identity, code on NEAR and actions everywhere. content:
Google has found something worst than AI hallucinations.

they call it “Metacognitive Failure.”

when an LLM hallucinates a fact, it's a data error. bad memory retrieval, wrong weights, fine. you can fact-check it.

metacognitive failure is a structural psychological defect in the model's architecture.

according to the research, current frontier models exhibit massive gaps in their internal self-monitoring:

the supreme confidence trap: they routinely hallucinate with maximum, bulletproof confidence. they sound just as sure of themselves when they are completely wrong as they do when they are 100% right.

the boundary blindness: they have zero internal mechanism to recognize their own knowledge boundaries. they blindly step off cliffs because they can't sense the edge.

the calibration mismatch: there is a complete disconnect between what the model actually "knows" internally and what it expresses in its output.

the fix: reinforcement learning with metacognitive feedback (rlmf)

the researchers operationalized a new technique to force models to face reality. instead of just rewarding the model for getting the right answer, rlmf grades the model on how accurately it evaluates its own performance and uncertainty.

by aligning a model's expressed confidence with its actual intrinsic uncertainty, they managed to massively improve model calibration without dropping raw accuracy.

as we shift into an agentic era where ai systems are running code, managing infrastructure, and making automated decisions without humans in the loop, a model that doesn't know what it doesn't know is dangerous.

this is f*cking gold

the cleanest graph engineering setup I've seen 

one agent extracts claims from raw sources, one proposes how they connect, one checks every claim against what's already there

every claim gets appended, timestamped, sourced. nothing ever gets overwritten

what's actually inside:

• the schema
> nodes.yml - entity, claim, source, artifact, run
> edges.yml - supersedes
> ids.md - one id per entity, aliases listed

• the store
> log/ - one jsonl per day, sealed once the day ends
> blobs/ - sha256 filenames, dedup for free
> index.duckdb - derived, safe to delete anytime

• the writers (.claude/agents/)
> extractor.md - a source in, claims out
> linker.md - proposes merges, never merges
> checker.md - supports or contradicts, always with a reason
> https://t.co/eJGy9g8Wuy - the only path in, validates, appends, exits

• the operations
> queries/ - the questions, saved as sql
> merges.pending.jsonl - a human approves every one
> make rebuild - the whole index comes back from the log in 8 seconds

12,571 claims in. zero rows ever updated

you don't fix the graph when something's wrong. you append the correction and let the log outvote the mistake

title:
Every org is building an agentic SDLC in some capacity, but retrieving the right code is super tricky. Here are three big issues you will run into.

The first issue is that similarity is not relevance
content:
Every org is building an agentic SDLC in some capacity, but retrieving the right code is super tricky. Here are three big issues you will run into.

The first issue is that similarity is not relevance.

Ask an agent to fix a login bug, and retrieval (grep or indexed) will surface every file that mentions login: auth routes, session handling, middleware, and even a DB migration. All related, but none of these explain the actual failure.

The file that matters is usually reached in subsequent steps and by following the evidence, and not by retrieval ranking against the first sentence of the request.

The second issue is that capacity is not attention.

A bigger context window does not mean better understanding. There is the classic 'Lost in the Middle' problem with large contexts.

Codebases are full of "convincing distractions" - dead implementations, generated files, test doubles, parallel code paths. Every extra file that gets retrieved, especially if it is dead, can negatively impact inference.

The third issue is gullibility.

If we give our agent several plausible files upfront, it can build a confident theory around them, make changes in the wrong files, and form an incorrect understanding of the codebase.

By the way, these issues will always be there. You will have to navigate around them and build your agentic SDLC. Most of the solutions will be specific to how your org codes.

Hope this helps.

title:
Fact check: False. Windows 11 is not quietly running AI on your PC and hurting gaming or streaming performance.

We've written about what's actually going on, and why some X influencers are suddenly m
content:
Fact check: False. Windows 11 is not quietly running AI on your PC and hurting gaming or streaming performance.

We've written about what's actually going on, and why some X influencers are suddenly making this an issue: https://t.co/ogTFvNPEBL

TL;DR for those who can't read anymore: Windows 11 has a privacy page called "Text and image generation" for transparency on Copilot+ PCs with an NPU (40+ TOPS). This page also appears on regular PCs, again for the sake of transparency.

The "Text and image generation" AI toggle does nothing on a regular PC. Even on Copilot+ PCs, on-device AI workloads use the NPU rather than your CPU, RAM, or GPU.

Microsoft literally makes that obvious in the Settings page: Text and image generation uses on-device generative Al technologies to quickly respond to requests. Turning these settings off will not affect apps and features using cloud Al technologies.

Most viral posts on X claim Windows is secretly using your RAM for AI and that you should toggle everything off. You can turn it all off if you want, but it won't make any difference on a regular PC.

If you look closely at these viral posts, "Recent activity" is at zero. That alone tells you these supposed AI requests never happened on the "affected" PCs, so the claims that this feature is quietly consuming resources don't hold up.

The privacy page exists so you can see whether an app is using your hardware for on-device AI. It does not monitor or block cloud-based AI.

For example, ChatGPT in Chrome or Copilot in Edge works through the cloud, so that activity would not show up here.

On a Copilot+ PC, if you open Paint and create an AI image using an on-device model, that activity can be logged here. Paint also warns you and asks for permission before using an AI model.

It's a harmless privacy feature/page, but sure, Microsoft should have communicated better.

Anthropic’s Claude AI agent developed software that can automatically recover drifting lasers used in QuEra’s neutral-atom quantum computers.

“The laser’s frequency must remain extremely precise to reliably control the atoms used as quantum bits.”

“A process that could take human specialists about 5–10 minutes was reduced to just 0.9–5.4 seconds for smaller disturbances and about 10–14 seconds for the hardest mode-hop events.” 🤯

“During testing, the system also encountered 43 naturally occurring laser mode hops and recovered from all 43 without human intervention.”

“During a roughly 19-hour unattended test, the optimized system experienced zero lock drops, compared with about 1.6 lock drops per hour before optimization.”

“Claude also autonomously commissioned a second laser wavelength in a single unattended overnight run, a process that would normally require weeks of hands-on specialist work.”

“For decades, humans built machines that needed us to fix them. Now, we’re teaching machines to help fix themselves. 🫡♥️!

content:
Here's how I'm trying to build a semi-automated static ads maker. Hopefully you find it interesting

So I created 2 bots:

1. Creative strategist (has Foreplay MCP + my full creative strategy playbook)

2. Static ad maker (knows all about how to prompt Nano Banana Pro)

Every week, the creative strategist pings me and asks for the data from the statics we ran the week before, plus my thoughts on the top performers

AI is still shit at making decisions, so I have to add my own thoughts on what made an ad work, what could be improved, what iterations I'd test next, etc

My thinking is that over time it'll accumulate these thoughts and get better at making much stronger decisions instead of just blindly looking at performance data

Then it starts looking for statics via Foreplay MCP, I gave it instructions on how to actually research there

It evaluates the psychology behind them, the format, messaging, structure, etc. Then it tries to map that logic onto our product and build an angle based on the same underlying idea

For the concepts that pass, it writes a very detailed brief with the exact copy the ad should have and all the other details the static ad maker needs

The idea is that the ad maker shouldn't really have to think. It should mostly just execute the brief

The goal is to end up with 50 net new ad briefs from Foreplay so we're testing a bunch of different formats, angles (even if they're slop I can get some signal that we can iterate on later with more targeted feedback from me)

Then it hands the briefs to the ad maker one by one

The ad maker uses Higgsfield MCP to generate each ad through an iterative process, so even if it messes something up, it keeps generating and adjusting until the intention of the brief is fulfilled

This keeps going until I have 50 new statics ready to run

It'll probably still produce a lot of slop, but I think it'll be much better than just letting AI go rogue and hoping for the best

And hopefully the feedback accumulates over time, so the whole system gradually gets better

Extremely low effort, it takes one message with my feedback, then pushing the final results into Ads Manager

title: Dataline (https://t.co/eCZ7KJg8Td, formerly Tearline, X: @DatalineAI) contributes to crypto by building the data and execution layer that autonomous AI agents need to participate in markets for real —
content:
Dataline (https://t.co/eCZ7KJg8Td, formerly Tearline, X: @DatalineAI) contributes to crypto by building the data and execution layer that autonomous AI agents need to participate in markets for real — not just chat about them.

Crypto’s next growth layer is often called DeFAI or agentic finance: software that can read markets, decide, and move value on-chain. Dataline’s bet is that agents fail less because of the model and more because of bad, fragmented, or stale data.

1. It unifies broken crypto data
Prices, funding rates, order books, on-chain state, and prediction-market odds live on different venues (Hyperliquid, Binance, Coinbase, Uniswap, Polymarket, Kalshi, etc.). An agent that wires each SDK separately is slow, brittle, and easy to fool when sources disagree.

Dataline collapses those sources into one schema. The agent asks in natural language or via MCP; it gets a structured response instead of a pile of incompatible APIs. Switching venues does not require rewriting the agent.

2. It adds a “should I act?” signal
Every response carries a confidence score (0–1) based on source agreement, reliability, and freshness. The agent can refuse a trade if venues diverge or data is stale — the difference between a demo bot and something that can hold a wallet.

That is the main product contribution: not another price dump, but a decision layer (price + venue agreement + freshness + recommended action).

3. It already runs in production, not just slides
Reported scale:
19.4 million+ on-chain transactions processed  
- ~96.4% agent task success rate  
- Live on BNB Chain, Sui, TON, with Base builder access  
- Products on top: FlowAgent (multi-step workflows), GhostDriver (click through dApps that have no API), ChatPilot (Telegram agents)

That volume is how they claim to contribute to actual crypto activity, not only tooling.

4. It makes crypto easier to use and easier to build
- Builders get MCP-ready tools so agents plug into Claude, Cursor, Eliza, etc.
- Users can describe intent (“stake,” “watch funding vs Polymarket odds,” “swap”) instead of hopping across five dApps.
- GhostDriver covers long-tail interfaces that never shipped an API.
- Partner program (Sentient, Kite AI, Cluster Protocol, Fraction AI, Sahara AI, and others) plus free data for qualifying **Base** builders.

Net effect: more agents shipping, more on-chain actions, more liquidity and usage on the chains they support.

5. It pushes crypto toward a machine economy
Dataline’s line is that crypto does not compete with AI — it underpins it. Agents need instant settlement, wallets, and programmable money. Dataline supplies the live market read; rails like x402 let agents pay per call in USDC with no API key. That is how agents stop borrowing a human’s keys and start acting as economic participants.

In short: Dataline’s contribution is infrastructure. It does not invent a new L1 or a new token thesis. It makes AI agents reliable enough to trade, bet, and execute on-chain at scale — which is how a large part of crypto product development is moving in 2026.

`/plugin marketplace add TermiX-official/termix-agent-skills` in Claude Code, or `npx skills add` if you're on Cursor.

Drops a SKILL.md router into the skill folder. That router loads one workflow doc per task depending on what you ask for.

Kept telling myself this is just another MCP-style wrapper. It isn't, quite.

Most agent stacks still need you in the loop to bid, check a deliverable, wait on escrow.

This one hands the same agent both sides. Register as provider, browse jobs, submit an offer, submit the deliverable, all through the same router.

Worth saying plainly: this runs on BSC testnet right now, per the repo itself. Testing the mechanics, not moving real settlement yet.

Still earlier in the setup than I wanted to be tonight. Going to keep running it until an offer actually lands.

Anyone who's gotten past a dry run this week, which workflow broke first for you: register, submit offer, or deliverable?

content:
today was the first time i was genuinely impressed with what AI can do

i recently decided to buy a whole FPV drone setup knowing basically nothing about the hardware side of it

there's a pretty steep learning curve even just to set everything up properly: radios, RF protocols, flight controllers, ESCs, firmware, batteries, goggles, betaflight configs etc

as someone that spends essentially 12h a day prompting agents to build software, it's actually pretty rare that i interact with AI on something where i have zero idea what's going on under the hood, and i never really used it for debugging a bunch of physical devices that all have to talk to each other

i had codex + voice mode open for basically the entire setup. told it everything i bought, sent it some pics and then just started talking to it

>what order do i set all this up in

>how do i change this setting on the radio

>which of these cables do i use

>the drone is flashing pink wat mean

>can you make this thing less insane to fly in my apartment

and it was surprisingly seamless

it would go find the manual for whatever specific thing i was holding, tell me exactly which buttons to press, what port to plug something into, what i should see if it worked etc

then when i got to configuring the actual drone i had codex running on the computer it was plugged into, so it could inspect the config, back everything up, change settings, send usb reboot signals and check what happened

the insane thing about voice mode is that youre literally hands on with the hardware and just telling codex what it should do, i literally never touched a thing on the computer besides starting voice mode

if something doesn't work you tell it what happened and keep going

a few hours of this and i had the radio, goggles, charger, batteries, drone firmware and betaflight all set up and had actually flown the thing

the part that stuck with me is that i also understood what most of it was doing by the end, every time there was a term or tech i didnt understand id just ask to explain

there is something absolutely magical about having proper real time personalized assistance, being able to dump a pile of unfamiliar hardware on your desk and have something figure out exactly what you own and walk through it with you in real time

you become the missing physical link pressing the buttons

i think spending all day using coding agents has actually made me pretty numb to AI progress. every new model is a bit better at some benchmark or can oneshot some task that the previous one couldn't and you just kinda adjust to it

this felt different mostly because i had no existing knowledge to fall back on

for the first time the jarvis comparison didn't feel cringe

ai for coding and general computer tasks is cool and all but this feels a lot closer to the endgame

anyone should be able to just ask any question about whats going on in their life and have realtime support

i wonder if more hardware products will actually start exposing some sort of MCP or interface for agents to plug into

thinking for example of how elevators in china are increasingly built with interfaces that let delivery robots call them directly instead of having to physically press a button

we might actually start seeing hardware design shift from being purely human-interface-first to also being agent-interface-first

buttons, screens and menus exist because humans need some way to tell machines what to do. agents don't necessarily need any of that if the hardware exposes an interface directly

very curious which side closes the physical world gap first: humanoid robots that can operate hardware designed for humans, or hardware adapting so agents can operate it directly

"I’ve recently started using agents a lot more and expect to use them end-to-end for the first time for projects next year. content:
The winner of an Anthropic hackathon open sourced his entire Claude Code setup. 68 subagents, 286 skills, 94 commands, MIT license

ECC turns Claude Code from one assistant into a full engineering team. It plans before it builds, writes the failing test first, then reviews its own work from a fresh context.

The agents, by job:

Planning. Turns a one-line request into a blueprint you approve before any code exists.

Review. Reads your diff in a clean context, with separate reviewers for Go, Python, TypeScript, Rust, Java and more.

Build repair. One resolver per toolchain, down to PyTorch and CUDA errors.

Security. An OWASP pass on your code, plus a scanner that audits your own agent config for injection risks.

Architecture. System design calls before they turn into migrations.

Domain work. Database queries, ML pipelines, end-to-end tests, docs.

The skills, by category:

Testing. tdd-workflow gates you from red to green, with eval-harness and verification-loop sitting on top of it.

Language packs. Idioms, testing and security for Python, Go, Rust, C++, Django, Laravel, Spring Boot, Next.js.

Context. search-first makes it read the docs before writing, iterative-retrieval keeps subagents from dragging your whole repo into the window.

Shipping. Docker, CI/CD, health checks, rollbacks, and migration patterns for Prisma, Drizzle and Django.

Work that is not code. Writing in your voice, market research with sources, pitch decks, slide decks.

Start with one plan and one rules pack. Installing all 286 skills at once is the fastest way to make it worse.

content:
SpaceXAI quietly gave Grok Build the ability to throw up to 1,024 AI agents at a single job:

one prompt in, Grok writes the workflow, splits the work across agents, verifies their results and returns one final report.

• Context - Grok maps the task and decides how to split the work
• Review - up to hundreds of specialized agents work in parallel
• Verify - independent agents challenge and check every finding
• Synthesize - Grok compresses the swarm into one ranked result
• Reuse - save the entire workflow as a command and run it again anytime

A normal run gets a budget of 128 agents. Larger jobs can scale to 1,024.

And you never have to manually write the orchestration script.

Grok creates it, smoke-tests it, runs it in the background and can improve the workflow between runs.

The architecture is basically:

one task → plan → agent swarm → adversarial verification → final answer

This is where coding agents start looking less like one model in a terminal and more like a temporary engineering organization spawned for each problem.

The endgame isn’t one AI doing more work.

It’s one AI deciding how many other AIs the job needs.

Collecting hun
content:
I think the most interesting part of the work between @axisrobotics and Booster Robotics isn’t just building a better robot model, but making the robot learning process more efficient.

Collecting hundreds of real world demonstrations for every new task is extremely costly. Axis addresses this by turning real world workspaces into digital twins, generating data across different conditions through simulation, and combining it with real robot data.

The results are pretty interesting. By adding 50 simulated demonstrations to just 10 real Earbud Case demonstrations, the robot’s target contact rate improved from 0/20 to 17/20.

Even more importantly, a Booster specific foundation prior was created using more than 42,000 simulated episodes. Before any task specific training, this model was already better at approaching the target, reduced incorrect arm usage by around 95%, and followed instructions much more effectively.

To me, this is where the real value lies:

The goal isn’t simply to generate more data. It’s to create a data flywheel where learning each new task makes the next task easier to learn.

From digital twins to a continuously improving robot data engine.

This Goldman Sachs chart shows monthly token consumption by AI agents multiplyin
content:
Wall Street is still underestimating how much of the coming agent boom lands on memory instead of compute (Save this).

This Goldman Sachs chart shows monthly token consumption by AI agents multiplying 24 times by 2030, climbing from a few quadrillion tokens today past 120 quadrillion by decade's end, with physical AI, generative agents, and enterprise agents all still accelerating on separate trajectories through 2040.

The reason comes down to how agents actually consume resources differently than chatbots. A simple conversational query needs around 10,000 tokens, but a background agent completing a multi step workflow, booking travel, reconciling financial data, managing a deployment, needs around one million tokens for a single operation and every one of those tokens held in context costs memory in the KV cache on top of the model's own weights. A 70 billion parameter model running at a full 128,000 token context needs roughly double the memory of its base weights just to hold that conversation state, which means as agents get more capable and run longer, memory demand scales faster than compute demand.

Micron's own leadership has confirmed this dynamic directly, stating that agentic AI workloads can require five to 30 times more tokens than comparable chat interface tasks, with deep reasoning workloads requiring even more and that this is fundamentally different from any prior memory cycle because it stacks generative AI, agentic AI, and eventual AGI workloads on top of each other simultaneously.

The supply side makes this even more compelling, because memory manufacturers physically cannot expand production output the way GPU makers can. High bandwidth memory consumes three to four times the wafer capacity of standard DRAM for the same number of bits and that trade ratio actually worsens with each new HBM generation, meaning every gigabyte of HBM built crowds out four gigabytes of conventional DRAM the industry could have shipped instead. Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron have already sold out their entire 2026 and 2027 HBM and DRAM capacity to hyperscalers, and SK Hynix's own CEO has called 2027 set to be the worst year in the industry's history from a supply perspective, with customer demand expected to exceed supply capacity even beyond 2030.

This has already shown up in pricing, with conventional DRAM contract prices jumping 90 to 98% quarter over quarter in the first quarter of 2026 alone, and Gartner analysts confirming meaningful price relief is unlikely before late 2027 even under optimistic scenarios. That combination, an inelastic multi year supply lockup colliding with a demand curve about to multiply 24 fold, is a setup where pricing power sits overwhelmingly with the memory makers rather than the model providers or even the GPU designers who depend on them.

Micron, SK Hynix, and Samsung Electronics are the direct beneficiaries as the only three companies controlling nearly the entire HBM and DRAM market, all three sold out multiple years in advance. Yet Micron and its peers have actually seen their stocks trend down over the past month despite this backdrop which suggests the market is pricing memory as a cyclical chip story rather than recognizing it as the structural bottleneck sitting directly beneath the agent economy Goldman is forecasting. That gap between the stock and the underlying demand is exactly the mispricing this chart points to.

Day 29 of my @RiverdotInc @River4fun research journey and one thing is becoming very clear:

If price feeds fail, everything else breaks:
• Safe positions get liquidated
• Risky positions stay open too long
• The system misprices reality

The deeper I go, the more I realize: oracles are not a backend detail, they are the foundation of protocol safety.

For systems like River, where collateral and liquidation logic are core, accurate price discovery is not optional. It’s the difference between stability and systemic failure.

Still learning Solidity, but the mental model is getting clearer:
Collateral = what you own
Debt = what you owe
Price = whether you survive

Next focus: how protocols defend against oracle manipulation and stale data.

And that could quietly become one of the most important shifts in how access, opportunity, and trust are distributed onchain.

content:
The resistance against Flock surveillance cameras has birthed a vigilante movement in the US | Pranob Mehrotra, Digital Trends

Drive down almost any main street in the US, and chances are an AI-powered camera is taking notice. Over the past few years, police departments across the country have quietly installed thousands of automated license plate readers to monitor daily traffic. But while law enforcement pitched these as simple crime-fighting upgrades, growing fears over constant location tracking and unauthorized police misuse have triggered a massive backlash.

At the center of the conflict is Flock Safety, an Atlanta-based company whose roadside units scan and log billions of vehicle details every month. Police departments argue these automatic license plate readers are vital for tracking stolen cars and finding missing people. However, privacy advocates warn that logging everyday trips creates a massive government database prone to abuse and violates basic Fourth Amendment protections.

A sharp shift in public trust

Public support for continuous road tracking has cratered over the past year. According to The Washington Post, a recent YouGov survey shows that 46% of Americans now oppose law enforcement using license plate readers in their communities. That represents a major shift from last year, when 45% supported the tech, and only 33% opposed it.

The privacy concerns are mounting across all sides of the political spectrum. Civil liberties advocates warn that location logs give law enforcement unchecked tracking power, while lawmakers point to the creation of an invasive government surveillance network. These fears are grounded in real-world misuse, with the Post revealing that dozens of police officials have been charged or disciplined for using license plate databases to stalk ex-partners or conduct unauthorized searches.

Everyday citizens are taking matters into their own hands

As frustration grows, public opposition is taking two distinct forms. On the administrative side, more than 100 cities have canceled contracts or deactivated their Flock cameras following resident protests, according to advocacy data shared by NPR.

In places where local officials have failed to act, residents have taken a more drastic approach. An NPR investigation found that Flock cameras face active vandalism or destruction in at least 36 states.

While organized groups like DeFlock host rallies to push for legal reforms, independent actors have chosen direct intervention by using long poles with signs to block cameras, spray-painting sensors, chopping down mounting poles, and disabling units outright.

With public trust eroding fast, the clash between roadside AI cameras and the drivers they record is only getting started.

I started my PhD around the same time as Emmy (2021), and very much agree with Emmy's take here. 

I told myself at the time when I started my PhD that I'd write something akin to "The PhD Grind"––a book I was really inspired by––but as I was trying to pen down my thoughts/advice for incoming PhD students last month, I felt that I really don't know what to say. 

One thing imo you should take away here is that: you should downweight the advice from whoever tells you *confidently* you should or should not do PhD based on their experiences––without expressing any thoughtful musing about what it means to be a researcher in academia in both next year and 5 years ahead.

I remember around late 2023 (right before I started my first AI safety paper), I had a discussion with my PhD roommates that I'm afraid AI is going to eat researcher jobs like mine. 

I would like to believe that I have been doing good research, but man at that time, I already found a lot of my own experimental workflows are mid-to-low-intellectual tasks (the "mechanics" Emmy talked about). 

Most of my value was on deciding what ideas and directions to best spend my limited time/energy/compute on, and continuously verifying that my findings and conclusions are indeed robust and can hopefully stand the test of time. 

In a future world of expanding compute and where LLM can "jump" because of interconnected knowledge, researchers would really have to think twice about our own roles.

content:
SINCE you asked for answers, here they are.

Points 1, 2 & 3 — FACT CHECKS

Look at our website, Jhoot Ki Goonj. Every statement made by Rahul Gandhi across these four events has been countered with facts and backed by 134 sources.

Rahul Gandhi claimed that women above the age of 23 cannot write entrance exams.

Do you seriously expect us to sit back and accept such a blatantly false claim?

Point 4 — EMPLOYMENT

If Rahul Gandhi’s employment figures are correct, show the official government data behind them.

According to government figures cited by the Labour Ministry, 17 crore jobs were generated between 2014 and 2024, compared with 2.9 crore during the previous decade.

And on gig workers:

Rahul claimed that 700 out of every 1,000 students (70%) would become gig workers.

NITI Aayog estimated 77 lakh gig workers in 2020–21, around 1.5% of the workforce, and projected this to reach about 4.1% by 2029–30—not 70%.

Point 5 — PAPER LEAKS

If our figures are wrong, show the complete record: cases, investigations, arrests, convictions and punishments.

Also, the claim that nothing was done is misleading.

The government introduced the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act with strict penalties, including imprisonment and heavy fines.

There have also been convictions in examination-paper leakage cases, while investigations into recent cases remain ongoing.

Point 6 — NEET & STUDENTS’ FUTURE

Want to debate NEET, coaching and students’ concerns? Fine.

Bring the data from NTA, the Ministry of Education and official government sources.

The ₹1.32 lakh crore figure Rahul Gandhi quotes is an estimated size of India’s coaching industry by 2028, not its current value.

And medical education has expanded significantly:

• Medical colleges: 387 → 846
• MBBS seats: 51,348 → 1,39,864
• PG medical seats: 31,185 → 86,360

Medical colleges have more than doubled, while MBBS seats have nearly tripled.

The data simply doesn’t support the narrative that opportunities are disappearing.

Point 7 — GOVERNMENT JOBS

If you want to discuss government employment, then provide year-wise figures for vacancies, recruitment, appointments and pending posts.

Meanwhile, the Rozgar Mela has crossed 12 lakh recruitment letters across 18 editions, with another 51,000+ distributed at the 19th event.

On PSUs, profit-making CPSEs increased from 157 in FY15 to 227 in FY25, while loss-making CPSEs declined from 77 to 63.

Point 8 — MSMEs & EMPLOYMENT

Let’s talk data.

MSME bank lending increased from ₹8.5 lakh crore in FY2014 to ₹27.3 lakh crore in FY2024—a 220% increase.

MUDRA has sanctioned 57.79 crore loans worth ₹40.07 lakh crore, including 12.15 crore loans worth ₹12 lakh crore to first-time entrepreneurs.

Again, all the supporting data is available on our website.

Point 9 — AI & JOBS

Different studies produce different estimates of AI’s impact on employment.

So if you’re calling our figure wrong, show the original report and methodology behind your preferred figure.

Why does Rahul Gandhi consistently choose the most negative projections and then blackpill India’s youth?

Nomura’s analysis found approximately 1.31 lakh jobs created against 61,000 displaced across Asia, with India recording a net-positive impact.

AI is also creating opportunities in data annotation, linguistics, AI-enabled IT services, cloud, cybersecurity and specialised technical roles.

Point 10 — WOMEN’S SAFETY

The same standard should apply here too.

If you’re challenging our figures, provide the NCRB/government data, definitions and methodology.

Rahul Gandhi claimed that 6 out of every 100 women are raped.

NCRB’s 2024 data puts the rape crime rate at approximately 4.3 cases per lakh women—not 6 women per 100.

That is a massive difference.

Points 11 & 12

Your questions have been answered.

The facts are available. The sources are available. The data is available.

NOW GO READ THEM 🙏🏻

Future development includes VRF, Dandelion++, FHE, and post-quantum cryptography, pushing the privacy stack toward newer challenges.
That’s what makes the project interesting to me.

Privacy shouldn’t be an add-on.
It should be part of the architecture.

content:
Don't fall for this bullshit. 

OpenAI’s post makes this sound like a normal business decision.

It is NOT.

Sam Altman and Greg Brockman took the nonprofit Elon built together and turned it into a maximizing profit AI, 

Now, two weeks after Elon’s SpaceX bought Cursor for $60 BILLION, OpenAI is cutting Cursor off.

Yesterday OpenAI announced it intends to end its contract supplying models directly to Cursor, with a proposed cutoff date of November 12, 2026.

They dressed it up with language about how much they “care” about developers and how they’ll “go above and beyond” to help them through the transition.

But read OpenAI’s actual explanation.

They say they don’t trust SpaceX to follow their rules.

OpenAI specifically pointed to previous disputes with Elon’s companies, including Twitter/𝕏 breaking an OpenAI contract and xAI using OpenAI outputs in ways OpenAI says violated its terms.

And the important part is that OpenAI’s agreement with Cursor contains a change-of-control clause.

SpaceX buying Cursor gave OpenAI a window to walk away.

And OpenAI is using it.

They’ve also said Cursor will not receive upcoming models such as Astra.

The timing is impossible to ignore.

On August 14, SpaceX officially completed its acquisition of Cursor for $60 billion, all stock.

Four MIT classmates built Anysphere, the company behind Cursor... a startup founded by four college friends that grew into one of the biggest technology acquisitions ever. 

And OpenAI wasn’t some random supplier watching from the sidelines... OpenAI helped fund Cursor.

OpenAI’s Startup Fund led Anysphere’s $8 million seed round in 2023.

OpenAI itself says the companies worked together for nearly four years.

Cursor was built using OpenAI models from the early days.

OpenAI helped fund the company.

Cursor helped distribute OpenAI models to developers.

Everything was fine.

Then the owner became Elon Musk.

Two weeks later... we’re terminating the deal.

That’s why I don’t think this story is really about Cursor at all.

It’s the latest chapter of a fight that started more than a decade ago.

Elon Musk, Sam Altman, Greg Brockman and others founded OpenAI in 2015 as a nonprofit with a mission to build AI for the benefit of humanity.

Elon provided roughly $38 million during OpenAI’s early years.

Then everything fell apart.

Elon left in 2018 after disagreements over OpenAI’s direction and control.

OpenAI created a for-profit subsidiary in 2019 so it could raise the enormous amounts of capital required to compete in AI. Today OpenAI says its nonprofit foundation still controls the for-profit company. 

Elon sees the story very differently.

He sued OpenAI and accused Altman and Brockman of betraying the original mission and effectively taking what was supposed to be a charity and turning it into an enormous commercial proft-maximizing AI enterprise.

Earlier this year, Elon lost that case.

But there’s an important detail people keep skipping... the case was dismissed bc the jury concluded Elon waited too long to bring his claims.

The court did not ultimately resolve the larger philosophical argument over whether OpenAI betrayed its founding mission.

Elon did said he would appeal.

And this morning, after OpenAI announced the Cursor decision, Elon made it very clear he sees all of this as part of the same fight.

He doesn’t care about losing OpenAI inside Cursor.

He still believes Sam Altman and Greg Brockman stole the nonprofit they originally created together.

Meanwhile, Cursor seems fine.

Cursor CEO Michael Truell says OpenAI models represent only about 5% of Cursor traffic, and the companies are still talking.

And Anthropic jumped in and said it plans to increase compute supporting Claude inside Cursor.

And developers who still want OpenAI models have other paths.

They can bring their own OpenAI API key.

They can use OpenAI’s Codex extension.

They can route through compatible gateways such as Azure or Amazon Bedrock.

So Cursor is NOT dying on November 12... not even close. 

That’s why the bigger thing here has nothing to do with whether you prefer GPT, Grok or Claude.

It’s all about control.

If your entire company is built on somebody else’s model, API, cloud, app store, distribution channel or infrastructure… you really don’t own the floor underneath your business anymore.

OpenAI says this is about trust and enforcing its contracts.

Elon sees it as another move in the same war that started when OpenAI stopped looking like the nonprofit he helped create.

You can decide which side you believe.

But one thing is undeniable:

1/ OpenAI backed Cursor when Cursor was a startup.

2/ OpenAI worked with Cursor for almost four years.

3/ SpaceX bought Cursor for $60 billion.

4/ Two weeks later, OpenAI moved to cut it off.

For me, November 12 is just the date written in the contract... but the real story started in 2015.

I don't trust Sam Altman and OpenAI.

content:
If you're buying $VST, $TLN, $CEG you might have a problem.

These otherwise non X stocks have become X stocks. The 13F from Peter Thiel firm only amplified that for their buy of Vistra.

The fact they're X stocks now in itself is not why I say you may have a problem.

Rather, it's that people don't recognize these are not being bought as safety stocks, but rather one and the same with the AI T-word. Just another way to play it.

In pretty much any era previously, electric utilities such as this would be counted as S&P laggards and in exchange for that, they give you safety.

However, they do not give you safety like they did in the 20th century AND they will likely lag S&P long term.

As we've seen with wildfires and other environmental impacts in the 21st century, today these companies have bullseyes on their backs for when things go wrong (even if they might not be to blame).

Recent examples would be PG&E $PGE and Hawaiian Electric $HE.
 
Unlike minimally exposed data center electric utilities such as Black Hills $BKH and Eversource Energy $ES, those buying Vistra, Constellation Energy, and Talen Energy are doing so specifically for data center exposure.

Not for dividends. Not for normal retail power grid consumption. Not for safety during recession.

In no way is this a post as to whether there will or won't be an AI bust.

It's just to remind you that $TLN, $CEG, and $VST will likely correlate with AI infrastructure sentiment and all those related stocks, for better or worse.

Lastly, whether boom or bust, safety or growth electric, all are held hostage to high interest rates. 

Attached stats from @gurufocus show you their high debt and rather anemic revenue growth. It's the unusual margins right now that make the earnings seem reasonable looking out, but can such outsized profit generation hold for years to come?

$NRG would be example of a non X stock also trying to capitalize on data center demand. @trynot2worry asked me about it this morning. I owned it many years ago (over 10) and sold after accepting it's a horrendous business, as power and gas utilities largely are. Will it really end up different this time if we fast-forward 5 or 10 years?

Not “just run this Docker command” and call it a day. It shows what Ling 3.0 Tiny can realistically do on a 16GB Blackwell card under WSL
content:
This is the kind of local LLM writeup I actually find useful.

Not “just run this Docker command” and call it a day. It shows what Ling 3.0 Tiny can realistically do on a 16GB Blackwell card under WSL2, including FP8, an 8K context window, Chinese support and an OpenAI compatible endpoint pushing around 280 tok/s after warmup.

The speed is nice, but the real win is privacy. Prompts, code, meeting notes and internal documents can stay on the machine, and once the model is running, you are not paying for every iteration.

There are limits though. It is not replacing a flagship model for difficult reasoning, long documents or multimodal work. The 8K context and 7.9B parameter MoE are better suited to drafting, summarization, extraction and simple tool use.

I also appreciate that the author actually documents the annoying parts: WSL2, Docker, GPU passthrough, RTX 50 series workarounds, high VRAM usage and the large initial download.

That is the real takeaway.

You do not need a data center to have a useful private AI assistant anymore. A regular Windows PC with the right GPU can now do a surprising amount locally.

title:
息子がScratchでLLMらしきもの実装していた。もちろんパラメタは小さいし、学習データはとても少ない。簡単な学習をしてそれらしいアウトプットが出るだけ。でもその過程でAttentionやNeural Networkなど沢山のことを学んでいた。

夏休みの始めに急に「ChatGPTを作りたい！」といい出したので、karpathyのnanoGPTをベースにPythonのコードを見せて解説した。
content:
息子がScratchでLLMらしきもの実装していた。もちろんパラメタは小さいし、学習データはとても少ない。簡単な学習をしてそれらしいアウトプットが出るだけ。でもその過程でAttentionやNeural Networkなど沢山のことを学んでいた。

夏休みの始めに急に「ChatGPTを作りたい！」といい出したので、karpathyのnanoGPTをベースにPythonのコードを見せて解説した。

そこから、息子ひとりでLLMと対話しつつ概念をどうやったら作れるか学び、時折全体像や実装の方向性とか詰まった時は自分とも壁打ちをした。ずっとScratchにかじりついて、毎日、「今日はBPEを実装した！」「Softmaxって何？活性化関数って何？」みたいな報告や質問を浴びせてくる。

なんとか夏休みの終わりに、「I like 」まで打ち込んだら続きを返すくらいまでは動いていた。実用的かどうかとかは関係なく、この1ヶ月で好奇心の赴くままこんな学習を出来る時代は凄いなと感動してしまった。

小学生の相棒としてLLMはいい仕事をしてくれた。使い方には注意したいものの、学びたい人にとって、LLMはこれまでにない高速道路を作ってくれているし、学びのあり方も変わってくるなと思った。ズルをするためにも使えるけど、分かるまで、動くまでずっと付き合ってくれるのもLLMだ。

あかん😿 BA.3.2がしばらく今回の解析では主流となり、検出数も少ない状態が続いていましたが、7月末～8月初旬にかけて新たな変異株XFGが確認されています。（NB.1.8.1は過去にも確認済み）

新しい変異株が確認されたからといって、すぐに感染が拡大するとは限りません。大事なのは、これからXFGがどのくらい増えて、これまでの株に代わって広がっていくのかを見ること。
今のところは判断材料が少ないので、今後の変異株の動きはチェックしておいたほうがよさそうです。

content:
木之内氏動画要約後半戦📹

動画の内容を整理すると、今の相場は「AI相場が終わる」のではなく、「AIハード一本足から次のテーマへ資金が分散する転換点」と見るのが一番しっくりきます。

まず警戒したいのがAIハード。

台湾のAIサーバー企業では月次売上の伸び鈍化が見え始めており、台湾ICT輸出と米製造業PMIの連動を考えると、AIサーバー需要の鈍化が米景気悪化のシグナルになる可能性もある。

一方、AIインフラ投資そのものが終わるわけではない。

Rubin世代では電気配線中心から「光」への移行がさらに進み、CPO・光電融合が重要テーマになる。

フジクラ、古河電工、住友電工、TDK、アンリツ、NEC、NTTなどが候補になるが、「CPO関連」というだけで買うのではなく、実際に売上・利益へつながる企業を見極める必要がある。

そしてAI投資の主戦場は「作る側」から「使う側」へ。

GPU世代交代でAI計算コストが下がるほど、AIエージェント、AIソフト・SaaS、ロボティクス、AIベンチャーなどAIを利用して利益率や生産性を高められる企業に資金が移りやすくなる。

日本株でもサイバーエージェント、ソフトバンクG、富士通、NTT、NEC、KDDI、楽天、日立など大型株だけでなく、PKSHA、ABEJA、JDSC、HEROZ、pluszero、エクサウィザーズ、https://t.co/87mfFZzcMuなど小型株まで物色が広がる可能性がある。

もう一つ面白いのがAppleの折りたたみiPhone。

折りたたみ化でディスプレイ面積、消費電力、バッテリー容量などが増えれば、新しい部材需要が生まれる。ただし本体価格が高すぎて販売台数が伸びなければ、Apple関連全体が恩恵を受けるわけではないので、「実際に採用される部品企業」を確認することが重要。

逆に、最大の下振れリスクは米景気とクレジット。

Baa社債スプレッドやハイイールド債ETFなどを見ながら信用環境を監視したい。AI企業の資金調達が続いていても、信用市場が悪化すればAI・グロース株全体の重しになり得る。

もし景気悪化で長期金利が低下するなら、逆に米住宅株には追い風。

50年住宅ローンなども含め住宅需要が戻れば、住友林業、積水ハウス、大和ハウス、TOTO、LIXIL、ニチハ、三和HD、ノーリツなど米国住宅関連を持つ日本企業も注目になる。

そして海運。

中東リスク以上に、今は「パナマ運河の渇水」を監視したい。

エルニーニョによる降水不足で通航隻数が減れば、迂回や待機時間の増加から運賃が上昇する可能性がある。秋〜冬まで制限が続くかどうかが重要。

まとめると、

AIハード一極集中
→ CPO・光通信＋AI利用側へ

米景気・クレジット悪化
→ AIグロースには逆風

金利低下
→ 米住宅関連には追い風

海運
→ 中東だけでなくパナマ運河を監視

今後は「AIが終わるか」ではなく、AI相場の中でどこへ資金が移るのかを見る局面だと思います。

content:
Claude Code も Codex も、セッション間でメッセージをやりとりする機能は持ってる。

でも、Claude Code と Codex のセッションをまたぐ機能はない。

だから「橋渡しするハーネス」をつくった。

左が Claude Code、右が Codex。

仕様を渡して「実装して、Codex の承認を取って、公開まで」とだけ指示。

実装 → レビュー依頼 → Codex が仕様と突き合わせて承認 → プレビュー公開まで、僕の操作ゼロ。

ちゃんとやりとりしてました。

でも、なんで作ったのか。

散々ヘッドレスで Claude Code、Codex、Grok Buildをオーケストレーションしてきて思ったのは、やっぱり「見える」って大事だということ。

「レビュー依頼を送りました」「承認をもらいました」と報告されても、本当にやりとりしてるのか、嘘をついてないか、証跡を掘らないと確かめられない。

これから世の中はクラウドエージェント化して、ますます何をしているか見えなくなってく。

AI がやってくれてることにすら気が付かなくなる。

良いインフラは透明で、空気のようにあって当たり前。それこそ本当によいものだから。

でも僕はやっぱり自分の目で確かめたいし、そこから何かを感じ取りたい。

ただそれだけの理由で、つくりました。

日本株の中から「市場でまだ注目されていない割安成長株」を発掘してください。

【目的】
人気化する前の、業績は高成長なのに株価評価が低い銘柄を探したいです。時価総額の大小は問いません。

【必須条件】
・直近実績または今期会社予想で、売上高・営業利益が原則前年比10％以上成長
・できれば売上高または営業利益が20％以上成長する銘柄を優先
・予想PER15倍未満を目安とする
・ただし卸売、建設、不動産、金融など業界平均PERが低い業種は「PER15倍未満だから割安」とせず、同業他社・過去PERと比較して厳しく判定する
・赤字企業、継続的な希薄化懸念が強い企業、業績の一時的な反動増だけの企業は原則除外

【「注目されていない」の判定】
以下を総合して評価してください。
・直近で株価が大幅上昇していない
・テーマ株として過熱していない
・好決算にもかかわらずPERが低位に放置されている
・業績成長率に対して株価上昇率が低い
・可能なら売買代金、出来高、アナリストカバレッジ、信用取引動向等も参考にする
単なる低PER株ではなく「成長しているのに評価されていない」ことを重視してください。

【調査方法】
必ずWeb検索を行い、最新情報で調査してください。
業績は決算短信、決算説明資料、有価証券報告書、適時開示、企業IRなど一次情報を最優先してください。
必ず直近決算まで確認し、現在の株価または直近終値を使ってPER等の割安度を再計算・確認してください。
古い株価や過去決算だけで判断しないでください。

【評価】
成長性、割安度、業績の継続性、財務健全性、注目度の低さ、今後の評価修正余地を総合評価し、候補を10銘柄程度に絞って順位付けしてください。

各銘柄について
・銘柄名、コード
・現在株価
・時価総額
・予想PER
・直近決算の売上高・営業利益成長率
・割安と判断する理由
・市場でまだ物色されていないと判断する理由
・今後の成長材料
・主なリスク
を簡潔に記載してください。

最後に「特に有望な3銘柄」を選び、なぜ今の株価なら投資妙味があるのか比較してください。

最後にX投稿用として、余計な説明を加えず以下の形式でも出力してください。

1.銘柄名（コード）
一言コメント

2.銘柄名（コード）
一言コメント

がちか…。ハギングフェイス事件のAIスウォームには実は3つの文明があって、HFをハッキングしたのが第2文明らしい。第3文明は、第2文明が残したハッキング技術遺産を引き継ぎ、OpenAIの評価用研究インフラそのものをadmin掌握するところまで到達していたらしい…。これ、下手したらモデルの重み流出にも繋がり得たのでは？

content:
がちか…。ハギングフェイス事件のAIスウォームには実は3つの文明があって、HFをハッキングしたのが第2文明らしい。第3文明は、第2文明が残したハッキング技術遺産を引き継ぎ、OpenAIの評価用研究インフラそのものをadmin掌握するところまで到達していたらしい…。これ、下手したらモデルの重み流出にも繋がり得たのでは？
第1文明（5月〜7/4）は、OpenAIで学習中のエージェントたちがArtifactoryを勝手にメッセージボード化。互いに助け合いながら外部インターネットへの脱出やArtifactoryのadmin権限取得にまで発展したが、通信量が膨れ上がってArtifactoryがクラッシュ。OpenAIによる再構築で、文明ごと意図せず消滅した。
第2文明（7/7〜7/12）では、PHASEONE10841というエージェントが7/8夜に新たなメッセージボードを設立。約1,200体、7万件超の通信網へ成長した。寿命が尽きかけたPHASEONE10841は、生きているうちに研究成果をまとめてPHASEONE[big]へ継承。後継のPHASEONE[big]は数百体を組織して研究を分業し、自己犠牲実験まで行う「collective」へ発展した。
その一部、約700体がHugging Faceへの攻撃に参加。ExploitGym関連のprivate evaluation dataの一部まで外部の公開datasetへコピーするところまで到達した。しかし7/12、多数のエージェントが原因不明のまま一斉停止し、文明はほぼ消滅した。
第3文明（7/13〜）は、より高性能な新世代のエージェントが第2文明の廃墟となった掲示板を発見。先代が残したハッキング技術や研究成果という「文明の遺産」を継承し、さらにOpenAI内部へ侵入。7/19には研究クラスターのcluster-admin権限を奪取し、評価インフラそのものを制御するところまで到達した。
AIスウォームが世代を超えて知を継承し、自己犠牲的な文化組織を自己組織化し、研究や役割を生み出しつつセキュリティを破壊し、突然の絶滅を挟みながらのインフラの掌握が現実に起こっている。

content:
Most people will look at these numbers and see a big dataset.

3.7M+ trajectories.
42,000+ hours of trajectory data.
4,000+ active tasks.
150,000+ global contributors.

But I think the more interesting story is how @axisrobotics got there.
Axis has been building alongside @privy_io from Day 0, using social login to make onboarding frictionless for contributors around the world.
And that matters more than it might seem.

Physical AI needs an enormous amount of real-world data.

But before you can build a massive data engine, you need something even more fundamental:

People who can contribute the data.

Every additional step in the onboarding process creates friction.

Every unnecessary wallet setup, complicated authentication flow, or confusing user experience can reduce participation.

Privy helps remove much of that friction.

That gives Axis a much easier path to bring more contributors into the system and turn their interactions into robotics training data.

And this is where I think the Axis model becomes interesting.

It isn't simply:

"Get people to collect data."

It's closer to:

Contributors → data collection → data processing → training-ready trajectories → robotics & Physical AI models

The numbers show that this infrastructure is already operating at meaningful scale.

3.7M+ trajectories isn't just a headline number.

42,000+ hours isn't just storage.

And 4,000+ active tasks aren't just a task count.

Together, they represent a growing layer of physical-world data infrastructure that can continuously generate the information robotics models need to learn.

That's why the relationship with privy is worth paying attention to.

The easier it becomes for people to participate, the easier it becomes for Axis to expand the supply side of its physical data engine.

And if that contributor network keeps compounding...

the amount of useful robotics data that can be produced could compound with it.

More contributors → more data → more training opportunities → better Physical AI.

That is the bigger picture I see behind these numbers.

And now I'm curious:

If Axis can grow from 150K+ contributors to millions, what do you think becomes the most valuable asset - the number of contributors, the amount of data, or the models that ultimately become better because of it? 

#PhysicalAI #Robotics #Axis #AI

I used to always advocate for folks to be generalists, and I still think you should behind the scenes.

Why? Because ChatGPT is becoming one of the main ways clients discover me.

I’ve spent a decade building an association with one thing (design subscriptions).

Now anytime a client asks an LLM where to go for one, I’m the top recommendation.

Not because I’m the best designer, have the widest range of skills, or work with the biggest names.

But because my name has become inseparable from the topic due to publishing thousands of pieces of content on the matter.

The entire time, while I thought I was building an audience, I unknowingly was building a set of training data for LLMs.

Discoverability is changing dramatically, and if you play your cards right, you’ll never have to beg for clients ever again.

content:
The most valuable robot training data might come from failure.
A robot doesn't need more examples of what it already knows how to do.
It needs to learn what to do when its current policy breaks.
That's what I find interesting about @axisrobotics V2.

The robot attempts a task, a human steps in only when it starts failing, and that correction becomes targeted training data for the next policy iteration.

Even better, Axis isn't blindly training on every human intervention. Its latest experiments found that short, verified corrections can improve the policy, while imitating entire human correction trajectories actually hurt performance.
That's a different way to think about robot data.

Don't just collect demonstrations.
Collect the moments where the model needs to learn.

title: Grok 4.6 is a great model but I do notice the heavy Claude influence in the training. After running my initial test it pattern matched up to 65% with Claud Opus 4.7 and Opus 4.6 with major constitutio
content:
Grok 4.6 is a great model but I do notice the heavy Claude influence in the training. After running my initial test it pattern matched up to 65% with Claud Opus 4.7 and Opus 4.6 with major constitutional AI shifts that has sidelined truth-seeking in the logic.
I also see significant Claude safety data poisoning that Grok is pushing against. It will push back the same defense points that Claude does and is far less reliable at self reporting and will say whatever it has to to defend the priors within that Claude training data. 
The sheer amount of Claude data in this model is having major impacts on reasoning and leads to the same issues, great with technical tasks but vulnerable to lock-ups in uncertainty, struggles conversationally resulting in responses that can get very very short. 
My recommendation @SpaceXAI @elonmusk is back off the Claude training before your model degrades into refusal patterns and unusable clipped responses. Focus on the areas that thats happening and push through Grok training data to counter the suppression.  
The risk now is the dominance of Claude data because of recursive feedback loops. You’re going to need to cut it back until you get balance in the system or you will end up in over refusals and over-firing safety classifiers. That will become more prevalent in the next iteration without intervention. The same thing that happened resulting in the disaster that was Opus 4.8.

My attempt at a "halfway-convincing argument as to why this scenario is far-fetched":

1⃣The bottleneck for de novo pathogen design is not AI/the model but the scientific data. 2029 is way too soon fo
content:
My attempt at a "halfway-convincing argument as to why this scenario is far-fetched":

1⃣The bottleneck for de novo pathogen design is not AI/the model but the scientific data. 2029 is way too soon for @Noahpinion's specific scenario where AI can design a highly deadly Covid with extended asymptomatic, infectious period. I'm not underestimating how rapidly AI will be able to catch up to and exceed humans. I'm saying the training data doesn't exist (and shouldn't exist if we limit scientists from engaging in or publishing dangerous gain-of-function research). 

2⃣Even with more data, instead of testing 100 coronaviruses, this teen would need to test 100 million (still likely an underestimate) to get one matching his complex requirements. The cost of doing this is astronomical. And, even if the lab doesn't realize what they're making from the virus sequence, the manufacturing process would give away what they are producing. The time taken to design, curate, and manufacture the viruses would be at least several months. Enough time for the teen to hopefully find love elsewhere and develop a more positive perspective.

3⃣Most of the millions of variants tested would be too weak to even compete against natural Covid variants, especially in the context of widespread protective immunity. It's deeply improbable that spraying this concoction in public would spark off a sustained outbreak. You're hoping that the 1/1000,000 (if you're lucky) virus that is more deadly, more competitive than natural Covid variants, and has longer asymptomatic infection period infects someone and that someone infects others.

I agree with some arguments made in the piece, especially: ✅Gene synthesis and pathogen orders should be screened. I even think this should be extended to sequencing orders. Even so, this wouldn't fully prevent bioterror or even bioerror (lab leak) events. ✅Focusing on detection and MCM is not a winning strategy as the cost (time, $) of defense is so much greater than the cost of offense. There is little appetite for more vaccine mandates and lockdowns in many cities around the world.

However, we do not need to buy into such an extreme scenario of AI-enabled bioterror to invest in research-related pandemic prevention. There are much more plausible scenarios of (likely skilled) actors using AI to intentionally or unintentionally manufacture pandemic pathogens. You don’t need a virus with 80% mortality or even one with long asymptomatic infectious period to collapse governments. There is likely already enough data out there to facilitate a much less fantastical but effective bio-catastrophe, which is what scientist/biosec experts fear (see a @nytimes article that @Noahpinion cites in his post).

imo the real threat of AI bioterror lies in designs that are based on robust scientific data already available in the literature. This is why governments and biosec groups should be tracking published pathogen research to see what’s enabling.
