title: A US court ruled the First Amendment protects possession of AI-generated child rape media, “no real child appears in them.” This makes it harder for investigators who are already struggling with child
content:
A US court ruled the First Amendment protects possession of AI-generated child rape media, “no real child appears in them.” This makes it harder for investigators who are already struggling with child rapists distorting real images to look like AI. #OpDeathEaters
--------------------------------------------------------

A federal appeals court struck down the US ban on possessing AI-generated child rape media inside the home on 25 August, holding that the First Amendment protects such material where it depicts no real child.
The Seventh Circuit affirmed the dismissal of one count against Steven Anderegg, 42, of Holmen, Wisconsin, whose prosecution the Justice Department brought in May 2024 as its first federal case over child rape media generated entirely by artificial intelligence.
Judge John Lee, writing for a panel that also included Doris Pryor and Joshua Kolar, held the possession provision of 18 U.S.C. § 1466A unconstitutional as applied to Anderegg across 27 pages. Lee, joined by Kolar, filed a separate concurrence asking the Supreme Court to revisit the 2002 decision that controls the question.

Section 1466A(b)(1) is the provision that reaches a person who obtains obscene synthetic child rape media without producing it or passing it on. Prosecutors in the circuit covering Wisconsin, Illinois and Indiana no longer have that count available where the images depict no identifiable child and stay inside the defendant's home.

How the case began
Meta reported an Instagram direct message to the CyberTipline run by the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children in October 2023, after Anderegg sent sexually explicit AI-generated images to an account belonging to a 15-year-old boy and told the boy in the same exchange how he had produced it.

Investigators executing a search warrant found Stable Diffusion installed on Anderegg's laptop, modified with add-on components that gave the model the ability to render human genitalia. The Justice Department put the total haul at roughly 13,000 images. Hundreds of them showed nude or semi-clothed prepubescent minors displaying or touching their genitals, alongside the curated text prompts and the negative prompts Anderegg used to keep adult bodies out of the output.

A grand jury indicted him on 15 May 2024 on four counts under § 1466A: production, distribution, transfer of obscene material to a minor under 16 and possession. Prosecutors put his maximum exposure at 70 years with a five-year mandatory minimum, and he was detained pending a hearing on 22 May 2024.

"CSAM generated by AI is still CSAM, and we will hold accountable those who exploit AI to create obscene, abusive, and increasingly photorealistic images of children," then-Deputy Attorney General Lisa Monaco said when the charges were announced.

The government conceded during the litigation that the images depicted no actual child and could not be traced to one. The concession took Ferber and Osborne out of the case and left Stanley and Free Speech Coalition to decide it.

Chief Judge James Peterson of the Western District of Wisconsin dismissed the possession count on 13 February 2025 and left the other three standing. Prosecutors took an interlocutory appeal. William Clayman and Ross Goldman of the Justice Department's criminal division argued it on 30 October 2025 against Joseph Bugni of Hurley Burish, who represents Anderegg. The panel took just under 10 months to rule.

A statute written for the last technology
Congress passed § 1466A in 2003 as part of the PROTECT Act, drafted in direct response to the Supreme Court striking down the Child Pornography Prevention Act the year before. Subsection (c) states that it is not a required element that the minor depicted actually exist. Subsection (f)(1) reaches any "digital image or picture, computer image or picture, or computer generated image".

Obscenity is the ingredient Congress added to keep the statute inside the constitutional line, and § 1466A(b)(1) bites only where the material meets that standard. Lee assumed for the sake of argument that Anderegg's images did, then held the statute still could not reach them in his house.

Two precedents, four rejected arguments
Stanley v. Georgia, decided in 1969, bars prosecution for private possession of obscene material at home, on the reasoning that government has "no business telling a man, sitting alone in his own house" what books he may read or what films he may watch. Lee wrote that the holding "was predicated on the location, the home", rather than on the character of what was found there.

Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition, decided in 2002, struck down federal bans on computer-generated abuse imagery involving no real child. New York v. Ferber and Osborne v. Ohio, which place abuse imagery of real children outside First Amendment protection altogether, rest on the permanent record of an actual child's abuse and the economic motive that distribution supplies to producers. No real child appears in Anderegg's files, so the panel held that neither case reaches his conduct.

Prosecutors offered four reasons to override Stanley, and Lee traced each one to a passage in Free Speech Coalition rejecting it. On the government's case that offenders use such imagery to groom children, Lee quoted the Supreme Court's answer that government "may not prohibit speech because it increases the chance an unlawful act will be committed at some indefinite future time".

 On the case that synthetic material normalises abuse, the Supreme Court had demanded a significantly stronger and more direct connection to actual harm. On the case that virtual images substitute for the real market, the Supreme Court had called the theory implausible, since producers would switch to fictional images and escape prosecution altogether. On the case that AI output has become impossible to tell from photographs of real abuse, straining investigators, the Supreme Court had written that government "may not suppress lawful speech as the means to suppress unlawful speech".

Prosecutors also told the court that § 1466A(b)(1) survives because it reaches only material shipped or transported in interstate commerce, an element Stanley's statute lacked. Lee rejected the distinction on the ground that the eight-millimetre reels seized from Stanley's desk drawer had almost certainly crossed state lines as well, and treated the commerce element as jurisdictional rather than a description of anything wrongful.

A footnote set out federal sentencing data showing that nearly 44 per cent of possession offenders had engaged in aggravating conduct, alongside a caveat that the social science on whether viewing such imagery causes contact offending remains inconclusive. Another footnote flagged morphed images, which paste a real child's face onto another body, as sitting closer to Ferber. The panel did not decide that question.

Counts one through three remain live, and the opinion leaves untouched any prosecution for producing or sharing the same files.

The concurrence
Lee wrote separately, joined by Kolar, that the court would "benefit from additional guidance from the Supreme Court regarding the intersection between the First Amendment and virtual CSAM", and that in the years since Free Speech Coalition the technology has reached a point where AI output is virtually indistinguishable from images of physical abuse. Only in recent months, the concurrence said, have the tools become good enough to fool the human eye.
Justice Clarence Thomas anticipated the problem in 2002. Concurring in the judgment in Free Speech Coalition, he wrote that "if technological advances thwart prosecution of 'unlawful speech,' the Government may well have a compelling interest in barring or otherwise regulating some narrow category of 'lawful speech'". Justice Sandra Day O'Connor would have upheld the ban on virtual imagery indistinguishable from the real thing.

Lee cited testimony that the influx of synthetic material imposes growing burdens on investigators and lets offenders disguise pictures of real children by making the images look computer-generated, which slows the identification of actual victims among the files police recover.

Researchers at the Stanford Internet Observatory, led by chief technologist David Thiel, reported on 20 December 2023 that LAION-5B, the open dataset behind Stable Diffusion, contained 3,226 suspected instances of child sexual abuse material, of which 1,008 were externally validated. LAION withdrew the dataset and published a cleaned version, Re-LAION-5B, in August 2024. Demand for AI-generated material can therefore raise demand for the real abuse imagery the models train on, Lee wrote, which is the harm Osborne was decided to prevent.

21 million reports
NCMEC received 21.3 million CyberTipline reports in 2025. More than 400,000 of them carried what the organisation calls a generative AI nexus, and more than 182,000 involved offenders possessing, generating or attempting to generate AI abuse material. NCMEC has categorised 158,000 images and videos as AI-generated abuse material since 2023 and identified more than 275 victims of it.

Riana Pfefferkorn of Stanford, who predicted before the indictment that prosecutors would fall back on obscenity statutes for AI cases, wrote to NCMEC on 29 January 2026 to flag what those totals conceal. A Bloomberg investigation had found Amazon's 380,000 reports flagged as AI-related contained no AI-generated material at all, but known abuse imagery surfaced while scanning training data. 

Nearly 80 per cent of all generative AI CyberTipline reports in the first half of 2025 involved no AI-generated abuse material, Pfefferkorn wrote, and the single checkbox that produced the figure had misled lawmakers and researchers for six months. NCMEC itself notes that more than 10 per cent of industry reports arrive with inadequate information.

The Internet Watch Foundation logged 3,443 AI-generated abuse videos in 2025, against 13 the year before, a count drawn from material its analysts assessed directly rather than from industry self-reporting.

The law elsewhere
State legislatures moved faster than the federal courts. As of August 2026, 46 US states criminalise AI-generated or computer-edited abuse material, more than half of those laws passed in 2024 and 2025, according to the tracker maintained by Enough Abuse. Colorado, Massachusetts, Ohio, Vermont and the District of Columbia have no such statute. Oklahoma, Utah, Arkansas and Florida reach wholly fictional depictions; most of the rest require an identifiable minor or the manipulation of a real image, which leaves them closer to the morphed-image question the Seventh Circuit declined to answer.
Section 163.1 of Canada's Criminal Code reaches depictions of imaginary children. The Supreme Court of Canada held in R v Sharpe in 2001 that "person" in the definition covers both actual and imaginary human beings, and upheld the possession offence subject to narrow carve-outs for private material a person creates and keeps for himself alone.

England and Wales criminalise pseudo-photographs under the Protection of Children Act 1978 and non-photographic prohibited images under section 62 of the Coroners and Justice Act 2009. The Crime and Policing Act 2026, which received royal assent on 29 April 2026, created an offence of adapting, possessing, supplying or offering to supply a child sexual abuse image generator, carrying five years. The same Act extended section 69 of the Serious Crime Act 2015, on paedophile manuals, to cover pseudo-photographs and prohibited images.

How the ruling was reported
The Federalist ran the headline "Judge: Child Sex Abuse Images Are OK If They're Made With AI" on 28 August, one of several treatments casting the ruling as a judge legalising synthetic child rape media. The decision reaches in-home possession alone, leaves production, distribution and transfer to a minor fully prosecutable and rests on Supreme Court precedent the panel said it had no authority to set aside. "We are not free to redraw them ourselves", Lee wrote of the lines the Supreme Court has drawn, adding that the court leaves to the Supreme Court the prerogative of overruling its own decisions.

Hans von Spakovsky of Advancing American Freedom said that "AI-generated images are now virtually indistinguishable from the real thing and some of these images may be created based on real child sexual abuse material".

The Justice Department can seek rehearing before the full Seventh Circuit or petition the Supreme Court, which under its Rule 13 allows 90 days from the entry of judgment to file for certiorari, putting the date at 23 November 2026 unless a rehearing petition resets the clock. No decision has been announced.

Anderegg still faces trial in the Western District of Wisconsin on the three surviving counts.

Where the ruling can still be challenged
The Office of the Solicitor General decides whether the United States petitions the Supreme Court, and it has announced nothing. Rule 13 allows 90 days from the entry of judgment, putting the date at 23 November 2026, and a timely petition for rehearing before the full Seventh Circuit would restart the clock from its denial. Both moves are discretionary calls inside the Justice Department that lost the appeal, and neither carries a public comment process.
S.3021, the ENFORCE Act, passed the Senate by unanimous consent on 16 December 2025 and was held at the House desk the following day, where it has sat for eight months without a scheduled vote. John Cornyn sponsored it with Richard Blumenthal, John Kennedy and Mike Lee. Constituents pressing for a floor vote have one named target each, their own House member.

The bill strips the statute of limitations from obscene depictions of child sexual abuse, requires sex offender registration, presumes pre-trial detention, mandates supervised release and tightens the knowledge element on interstate transport. None of that restores a possession charge for images depicting no real child. The obstacle in Anderegg is Stanley, not the drafting of § 1466A, and Congress cannot amend a Supreme Court precedent.

Colorado, Massachusetts, Ohio, Vermont and the District of Columbia have no statute reaching AI-generated or computer-edited abuse material, which leaves a live bill to write for residents of those five jurisdictions. Stanley was itself a Georgia prosecution, so a new state ban on possession inside the home meets the same barrier the Seventh Circuit applied. State law reaching production, distribution and possession outside the home is untouched by the ruling.

Nothing in US federal law matches the offence England and Wales created on 29 April 2026 of adapting, possessing, supplying or offering to supply a child sexual abuse image generator, carrying five years. An offence aimed at the tool rather than at the file in a person's house falls outside what Stanley covers, and no bill before Congress creates one.
LAION withdrew its dataset and published a cleaned version after the Stanford finding, on its own initiative. No US statute requires a model developer to audit training data for abuse material or to disclose what an audit found.

NCMEC's reporting form carries a single generative AI checkbox, which produced the 80 per cent miscount Pfefferkorn identified, and she has asked the organisation to replace it with granular options. Congress, the courts and the concurrence in this case all cite figures drawn from that form.

Overturning the holding itself takes the Supreme Court revisiting Free Speech Coalition and narrowing Stanley, which is what Lee and Kolar asked for in writing, or an amendment to the Constitution. No lower court in the Seventh Circuit can reach it

content:
A robotics data engine can collect millions of interactions and still face one uncomfortable question:

Who actually needs the data and what problem does it solve?

That, to me, is where the conversation around Physical AI gets serious.

Being part of training physical AI is not by merely saying it. Active participation is how best to contribute: ⤵️

https://t.co/Xj6XN1UBT5

Because more data isn't automatically better data.

A robotics company doesn't simply need a random pile of trajectories. It may need specific behaviors, environments, variations and task conditions that match what its models must eventually handle.

This is where @axisrobotics gets interesting.

AXIS approaches the problem by turning requirements into structured Task Packages; connecting scenarios, skills, variation and usable trajectories to a clearer downstream purpose.

That changes the question from:

"How much robot data do we have?"

to:

"Can we generate the data this particular Physical AI problem actually needs?"

And that difference matters.

The deeper challenge in robotics isn't merely collecting data once. Physical environments keep exposing new weaknesses, new scenarios and new capabilities that models need to learn.

AXIS is building around that reality through a dynamic pipeline where requirements can become tasks, tasks can generate data, and deployment can reveal what needs to be collected next.

The contributor network sits inside that loop.

Your contribution isn't just activity inside a simulator. It can become part of a larger chain:

Customer need → Task → Human contribution → Data → Training → Physical AI

It's my humble observation that real value isn't having the most data. It's having the infrastructure capable of repeatedly turning real-world problems into useful training data.

And as Physical AI enters more industries, that ability could become increasingly important.

@axisrobotics

content:
Good morning, friends ☀️

Robots do not only need more compute. They need better ways to learn from the messy reality they operate in.

That is what makes @axisrobotics interesting.

The real opportunity is not simply collecting millions of robot trajectories. It is creating a system where simulation, human demonstrations, evaluation, failures, and corrections continuously produce better training data.

Axis is pushing toward that kind of compounding data engine.

Its V2 approach with human-gated DAgger is especially interesting. Instead of having humans control every movement, intervention happens when the robot reaches a point where it is likely to fail.

That small design choice changes the value of failure.

A failed action is no longer just a bad outcome. It becomes a signal showing exactly where the model needs help.

This creates a powerful loop:

Robot acts → failure appears → human corrects → data improves the model → robot tries again.

The important shift is from data collection to data compounding.

And there is a relatable lesson here too. The best training data may not come from perfect demonstrations. 

It may come from the moments where systems struggle, because those moments reveal the gaps that matter most.

If @axisrobotics can turn millions of imperfect contributions into increasingly useful learning signals, contributor activity becomes part of the intelligence infrastructure itself.

That is a much bigger idea than simply gathering data.

The future of Physical AI may depend less on how much data we collect, and more on how intelligently we learn from failure.

content:
I used to think teaching robots required a robotics lab. Turns out, I was wrong.

You can literally sit with your laptop and teach a simulated robot how to perform a task.

No expensive hardware.
No lab coat.
No complicated setup.

Just you, a browser and a task.

You move the robot.
It records your actions.
Your corrections become trajectories.
Those trajectories become training data.

And this is where @axisrobotics gets interesting.

Because one person teaching a robot is useful.

Thousands of people teaching the same robot differently is a data engine.

Different people make different movements.

Different people solve problems differently.

Different people make mistakes and recover in ways a model may never have seen before.

Axis turns those interactions into a decentralized source of training data for Physical AI.

But the part I find most interesting is the feedback loop:

Humans → trajectories → training → robot attempts → human corrections → better training.

The robot gets another chance.

Then another.

Then another.

That compounding experience could eventually help robots become genuinely useful around humans not just impressive in demos.

Imagine machines handling dangerous jobs, repetitive tasks, warehouse work, or physical tasks that are simply too demanding for people.

That's the bigger picture I see with Axis.

**We’re not just teaching robots what to do.

We’re helping them learn how to do it better.**

And maybe that’s what the future of Physical AI actually looks like.

Not humans being replaced overnight.

Humans teaching machines until machines become useful enough to help us.

title: This a pretty solid 'art of the possible' article around moving from a single-player AI coding workflow to a system that helps you write software automatically -- and a pretty solid definition of the
content:
This a pretty solid 'art of the possible' article around moving from a single-player AI coding workflow to a system that helps you write software automatically -- and a pretty solid definition of the differences.

Lots of this post resonated with me (although admittedly I got a bit lost at the last ~30%)

I think there is a recipe by which you can:
- Describe what you are trying to build
- Describe your constraints (e.g. what good looks like, how you want to build)
- Add guardrails (e.g. automated tests that steer the agent)
- Add conditional human-in-the loop (e.g when this happens, let me inject some new context)
-  Add ability for external information (e.g. bug reports, feature requests) to affect the system (both *what* it should do and *when* it should do)

And end up with something that resembles a system that builds the software for you. The key trick here (which the article mentions both explicitly and implicitly), is that you have to do the above things in a way that captures:
- Your specific and moat-enabling goals for the system
- Your domain knowledge for the specific domain the system is meant for 
- Your flavor of software engineering / software architecture / software quality, etc. etc. 

This is the tricky part, because although these models can 'do this for you' - they can do *anything* for you -- they are just going to do it essentially at what the *average* looks like in all the training data it's seen. You def. don't want to just leave lots of things to the model, because you def. aren't going to succeed if you are just building the average.

Either way, a great post to get a bit more in the weeds on what this entire factory concept is. Like anything, lots of ways to do a thing like this. We are so early in it all, so take the bits you need and try it out.

Morgan Stanley expects the server share of total DRAM demand to rise from 37% in 2023 to 59% by 2028. 

In a few years more tha
content:
AI servers are turning into memory systems, and the mix shift is large.

Morgan Stanley expects the server share of total DRAM demand to rise from 37% in 2023 to 59% by 2028. 

In a few years more than half of all DRAM produced would go into data centers rather than PCs and phones.

The reason is visible in one rack. 
NVIDIA and Morgan Stanley figures put an AI server rack at roughly:

HBM at the top, 20.7 TB per rack, attached directly to the accelerators. It is the only layer fast enough to keep GPUs fed during training and inference. Fastest and most expensive.

DRAM next, 54 TB per rack. This is the working memory for CPU orchestration, agent workloads and general compute. Every server still needs a lot of it.

NAND at the base, more than 100 TB per rack and configurable. This holds model weights, training data and cached results.

Faster memory costs more and holds less. Cheaper memory holds more and sits farther from the chip.

NVIDIA designs the accelerators that create the HBM hunger. 
$MU
$SKHY
Micron and SK Hynix are racing to produce enough high-bandwidth and high-density DRAM. 

Server OEMs then pack those memory-heavy systems into racks that data centers can deploy.

The bottleneck is no longer only GPU availability. It is whether enough HBM and server-grade DRAM can be made and delivered while models keep getting larger.

The AI buildout is becoming a memory story as much as a compute story. The move from 37% to 59% is the cleanest signal of that.

Which layer do you think stays tight longest, HBM, server DRAM, or enterprise NAND?
$DRAM $EWY

A robot can do a million things and still learn almost nothing.

The hard part isn't getting a robot to produce actions. It's knowing which actions are worth learning from.

That’s why robotics data is so different from the data behind language models.

When an AI writes a bad sentence, you can simply discard it. With a robot, the failure has context. Maybe the grip was wrong. Maybe the arm took an inefficient path. Maybe the object moved unexpectedly. Maybe the entire task broke down.

That failure is information.

This is what I find interesting about @axisrobotics. The focus isn't just on producing huge amounts of robotic data, but on creating a loop where physical behavior can be observed, corrected, verified and turned into better training signals.

The process becomes:

→ Robot attempts the task
→ Weak behavior is identified
→ Human provides the right correction
→ The correction becomes training data
→ The policy improves
→ New weaknesses become visible

That is much more useful than simply making the dataset bigger.

Because eventually, the goal isn't for robots to have seen everything.

It's for them to keep learning from the things they still don't understand.

And that could be one of the most important pieces of the Physical AI puzzle.

content:
Inside Physical AI and Robotics: How Axis Robotics Solves the Industry’s Core Bottleneck

The AI industry is hitting a new structural wall. While GPUs are becoming cheaper and compute is scaling fast, Physical AI and robotics face a completely different crisis: a massive shortage of real-world training data.

Unlike Large Language Models (LLMs) that were trained on decades of internet text, robotics has no “internet of physical interactions” to scrape. The entire industry currently relies on roughly 2,000 hours of public manipulation data—a drop in the ocean compared to the estimated 100 million hours needed for a true "GPT-3 moment" in physical intelligence.

The Axis Robotics Solution: A Closed-Loop Data Engine

@axisrobotics is bridging this gap by crowdsourcing physical data through a Web3-powered infrastructure:

➤ 3 Core Products: A browser-based web simulation platform (10k+ valid trajectories/hour), a mobile ego-centric app launching Sept 2026 for first-person hand-tracking, and an automated data-to-model processing pipeline.

➤ 3-Layer Quality Control: Real-time submission validation, backend trajectory replay (to prevent bots/scripting), and batch-level policy testing to ensure data learnability.

➤ Crypto Integration: Uses Base, Solana (BitRobot), and Pi Network to mint on-chain Data IDs for provenance, verifying who contributed what while building user reputation.

➤ Current Traction: Over 100,000 global contributors, 2.1M+ collected trajectories, and active partnerships with hardware/industrial giants like AgiBot, Unitree, Geely Auto, and Lotus Cars.

Market Maker Perspective: Real Demand vs. Token Dynamics

Evaluating the model reveals key insights from market makers like Cicada:

➤ Durable Demand: The need for clean robotics data is genuine and long-term.

➤ The Token Dilemma: AI research labs pay for data contracts in fiat, not project tokens. Furthermore, naive DePIN emissions risk encouraging spam, which can poison training datasets if quality control isn't strictly enforced.

➤ The Takeaway: Crypto serves well as a borderless coordination and provenance layer, but data engines must prioritize real-world utility over token speculation to survive.

content:
【半導体メモリの需給ひっ迫は継続】
足元では契約期間が3～5年にわたるLTA（長期供給契約）を締結する動きが広がっており、構造的な需給ひっ 迫に対する顧客側の危機意識が浮き彫りに。

AI需要が拡大するデータセンター向けの先端製品のみならず、PCやスマートフォン向けなどの汎用品も供給不足が深刻化しており、中国企業の増産を考慮しても、2028年にかけて半導体メモリの需給ひっ迫が継続するとみている。主な背景は以下の三点。

１．エージェントAIによるメモリ需要の急増
複雑な情報処理を実行するため、計算処理の増大に伴って必要なメモリ容量が飛躍的に増加する見通し

２．技術的差異
CXMTが2026年に旧世代品「HBM3」の量産を「目指す」と表明する一方、グローバル大手は新世代品「HBM4」の量産を既に開始。特に先端品における技術差は大きく、大手がシェアを奪われる可能性は低いと見る。

３．米国による制裁
半導体分野における対中輸出規制の強化を目的とした法案も提出されており、中国産半導体が中国外の市場でシェアを高めるにはハードルが高い。特にAIデータセンターは産業の根幹や国家安全保障にも関わるため、ハードルはより高い。

content:
#IZAKAYA
【サイト内の情報を保存しておいてください】

IZAKAYA公式サイトが復旧しました。
アクセス不可はSSL証明書の期限切れが原因だったようです。
　　
ただ今回のことでわかったように、公式ページは、こんなふうにある日突然落ちます。
　
今回は運よく復旧しましたが、次も戻ってくる保証はありません。だからこそ、アクセスできる今のうちに証拠を保全してください。
　
マイページ内の記録は、自身にしか取れません。

◆【STEP 0】今すぐ記録を保存
　
① 管理画面のスクリーンショット
・保有資産残高の一覧
・出金申請の履歴（申請日時・金額・ステータス）
・レンディングの契約内容と期間
・入出金の全履歴
など
　
② 送金の記録
・入金時のトランザクションID
・送金先ウォレットアドレス
など
※画面から必ず控えてください。ブロックチェーン上に残るので、後から追跡できます
　
③ 運営とのやり取り
・受信メール全件（絶対に削除しない）
・問い合わせフォームに送った内容
・KYCで提出した書類の控え
など
　
※スクリーンショットは、日時が画面に写る形で撮ってください。
　
◆【STEP 1】警察署へ「被害届」を出してください
　
最寄りの警察署に上記の資料を持って行ってください。まず電話して窓口を聞きましょう。
　
被害届を出しておき、記録を残すことが目的です。
このとき必ずこう伝えてください。

「今後、刑事告訴も検討しています」
　
この一言があると扱いが変わるようです。被害届は「被害の申告」ですが、告訴は「処罰を求める意思表示」です。告訴を視野に入れていると伝えることで、単なる相談ではなく事件として認識されます。
　　
なお被害届を受理された際の受理番号と担当者名を控えておいてください。

◆【STEP 2】刑事告訴へ
　
今後、状況が変わった場合には刑事告訴も視野に入れます。具体的にはこういう場合です。
　
・出金の停止が常識外に長期化する
・サイトにアクセスできず、マイページにもログインできなくなる
・サイトが完全に閉鎖される
・まったく運営側と連絡が取れなくなる
・サービスが破綻した、あるいはハッキングされたと発表される
　
刑事告訴は被害者の権利です。個人でも当然に行えます。
　
そして警察が告訴を受理した場合、刑事訴訟法によって書類と証拠物を検察官に送付する義務が生じます。
受理されれば、捜査機関は動かざるを得ません。
　
ただし、そのぶん受理の際に告訴状の内容が厳しく見られます。通常は弁護士に依頼するのが一般的です。
とはいえ書き方を学べば個人でも進められます。まずは下記のようなサイトで手続きの流れを把握しておきましょう。
　
AIを補助に使うこともできますが、できれば提出前には弁護士や専門家のチェックを受けてください。
内容が不正確だと、かえって受理されにくくなります。
　
刑事告訴のやり方｜元刑事が解説する告訴状の書き方と手続きの流れ
https://t.co/C0d5Js5nKy
　
なお被害届も告訴も、必ずご自身で出してください。
　
誰かがまとめてくれるのを待っていても、あなたの被害は記録されません。
全国の一人ひとりの届出が積み上がって、初めて事案の規模を理解してもらえます。

・5年で1億貯めた投資家
content:
【驚愕】5年で1億稼いだ個人投資家kenmoさん、SNSで大合唱されてる人気銘柄を華麗にスルーして「誰もが売りたくて仕方ない最安値」を狙う逆張り戦法を推奨しつつ、最後は「SNSで誰も語らない地味な銘柄こそ至高」という逆張りの真髄を披露してくれた件ｗｗ

「300万円を1億円にした投資家kenmo氏に聞く、テンバガーを狙う視点と注目株 5選」の動画をアホかわいく要約すると、
・5年で1億貯めた投資家ニキが登場。次のテンバガー（10倍株）を探す極意を伝授
・と思いきや「自分は10倍になるまで持ち続けたことはない」といきなり白状。一周回って好き
・10倍株のパターンその1は「景気敏感株」。どん底からの急回復で数字だけ暴れる
・パターンその2は「大ヒット商品」。皆が知った後では遅く、若者の嗅覚が有利だとおじさん目線で解説
・パターンその3は「優秀な経営者」。構造改革で長期的に売上と利益を伸ばし続けるタイプ
・狙うべきは時価総額2桁〜3桁億円の会社。1000億円まで育つ余地があるかが勝負の分かれ目
・売上よりも「利益」が大きく変わるタイミングを狙うのが鉄則。結果は正直
・SNSで話題の銘柄はすでに遅い。誰も見ていない「視聴率の低さ」が最大のチャンス
・「絶対いける！」と自信満々で買った株は伸び悩み、人から聞いて違和感を持った株の方がよく上がる。投資の沼が深い

【小まとめ】
テンバガーの条件を完璧に語りながら、自分の過去の投資スタイルは短期乗り換えだったと明かすお茶目な解説動画

【つづき】
・いよいよお待ちかねの注目株5選を発表。視聴者、全裸待機中

・1社目はITサービスの「SHIFT」。すでに10倍達成済みだが、AI化への構造改革でさらに伸びると予想
・2社目はシニア女性向け雑誌の「ハルメク」。ファン株主の熱量が高く、優待をもらいながら長期応援する玄人向け
・3社目は小型ドローンの「リベラウェア」。赤字だが人が入れない危険な場所を飛ぶ社会貢献度MAXのロマン枠
・4社目は半導体関連の「Vテクノロジー」。次世代のDI露光装置が爆売れすれば一撃ドーンの可能性あり
・5社目はまさかの「SpaceX」。時価総額デカすぎだけど、AIの進化で宇宙覇権を握る最強企業になると予想
・テンバガーを狙うと意気込むのではなく、優待目的で放置してたら結果的に10倍になっていたのが理想の姿だと結論づける
・投資手法は時代で変わるので、過去のパターンを分析して引き出しを増やすことが重要だと締めくくる

【どこがおもろかった？】
・1億円稼いだガチ勢なのに「テンバガー取ったことない」と冒頭でカミングアウト。飾らない姿勢は神対応
・視聴者が一番知りたい小型株は「株価が動くから」と自主規制。大人の本気とコンプライアンスの壁
・誰も知らない銘柄を推奨しておきながら、最後の最後で超有名企業の「SpaceX」をぶっこむ急カーブ
・「狙って取るもんじゃない」と身もふたもない結論。企画の根底を覆す火の玉ストレート

【総まとめ】
テンバガーになる銘柄の法則や探し方を、過去の具体例とともに分かりやすく解説してくれました。
しかし後半の個別銘柄紹介では、大型株や未上場企業などイレギュラーな選出が多め。
具体的な銘柄に飛びつくのではなく、会社を分析する視点を持つことの重要性を説いています。
結局のところ、必死に10倍を狙うより、気長に応援できる会社を放置するのが一番だと気づかせてくれます。

【結論】
「10倍株の探し方を理論立てて教えつつ、結局は気絶投資法が最強だと教えてくれる動画」です。

9枚（1枚2回使用）の画像を使用、アクション性は皆無、シンプルな英語プロンプトも記載しておきます🎥

※制作過程
①Midjouneyで画像生成（一番大事）
②Grokにストーリーを伝える
③ストーリーを補強させる
④画像を分析させプロンプト出力

⑦SUNOでBGM生成
⑧動画編集（1分以内に調整）
⑨動画編集（字幕と音楽）

※英語プロンプト（ほぼ一緒）
👇️👇️👇️
第1話（1番・裁判官）
Keep the exact same woman as the reference image. Do not change her face, eyes, hair, or identity. Cinematic 6-second video, dark gothic atmosphere, teal-blue color grade, no music, no BGM. Slow subtle push-in. She looks into the camera and speaks in a low, clear English voice: "By this court… are you witches?" Sound effects only: faint room echo, soft fabric rustle, distant low wind.

第2話（2番・崖の女）
Cinematic 6-second video, photorealistic, dark gothic atmosphere, teal-blue color grade, no music, no BGM, no soundtrack. Use the reference image of the woman in a dark Victorian dress standing on a misty cliff above a rough sea. Strong wind moves her hair and skirt. She looks slightly downward. She speaks softly in a clear English voice: "The storm called me." Sound effects only: strong coastal wind, distant crashing waves. No music.

第3話（3番・廃墟の女）
Cinematic 6-second video, photorealistic, dark gothic atmosphere, teal-blue color grade, no music, no BGM, no soundtrack. Use the reference wide shot of the woman in a long dark purple gown standing among snowy ancient stone ruins in heavy fog. Very slow camera drift. She stands still in profile. She speaks quietly in a clear English voice: "I once guarded these stones." Sound effects only: cold wind through ruins, faint snow hush, distant stone echo. No music.

第4話（4番・広間の女）
Cinematic 6-second video, photorealistic, dark gothic atmosphere, teal-blue color grade, no music, no BGM, no soundtrack. Use the reference image of the woman in a dark Victorian gown standing alone in a vast foggy stone hall with columns and arches. Slow, almost still camera. She looks down. She speaks in a low, clear English voice: "This castle belongs to no one now." Sound effects only: hollow hall reverb, faint dripping, soft cloth movement. No music.

第5話（5番・天を仰ぐ女）
Cinematic 6-second video, photorealistic, dark gothic atmosphere, teal-blue color grade, no music, no BGM, no soundtrack. Use the reference profile close-up of the woman with reddish-blonde hair looking upward, hands on her chest. Subtle breath and a tiny tilt of her chin. She speaks softly in a clear English voice: "Still, I look up." Sound effects only: quiet breath, faint distant wind. No music.

第6話（6番・雨の女）
Cinematic 6-second video, photorealistic, dark gothic atmosphere, teal-blue color grade, no music, no BGM, no soundtrack. Use the reference close-up of the wet dark-haired woman in rain, purple ruffled dress, looking into the camera. Rain falls across her face. She speaks in a steady, clear English voice: "Soaked. Not broken." Sound effects only: rain on stone, dripping water, soft breath. No music.

第7話（7番・森の女）
Cinematic 6-second video, photorealistic, dark gothic atmosphere, teal-blue color grade, no music, no BGM, no soundtrack. Use the reference shot of the woman seen from behind in a misty dark forest. She stands still, then slightly turns her head to the right. She speaks quietly in a clear English voice: "I won’t run." Sound effects only: forest wind, rustling leaves, distant fog drip. No music.

第8話（1番・裁判官・再登場）
Cinematic 6-second video, photorealistic, dark gothic atmosphere, teal-blue color grade, darker and colder than the first scene, no music, no BGM, no soundtrack. Use the same reference portrait of the blonde woman with layered hair, blue eyes, dark blue lace blouse, dark scarf, and lace gloves. Slow push-in on her face. Her expression is colder and final. She speaks in a low, clear English voice: "All guilty. Let the mist take you." Sound effects only: deeper room echo, low distant rumble, fabric rustle. No music.

第9話（8番・狩人）
Cinematic 6-second video, photorealistic, dark gothic atmosphere, teal-blue color grade, no music, no BGM, no soundtrack. Use the reference image of the woman in a long dark coat standing in a smoky field, holding a pistol, with soldiers faintly visible in the smoke. Slow walk forward, smoke drifting. She looks down, then slightly ahead. She speaks in a calm, clear English voice: "The verdict is already given." Sound effects only: wind through grass, distant muffled voices, cloth and leather movement, faint smoke hiss. No gunshot. No music.

第10話（9番・狩人・発砲あり）
Cinematic 6-second video, photorealistic, dark gothic atmosphere, teal-blue color grade, no music, no BGM, no soundtrack. Use the reference image of the woman by the old stone wall aiming a pistol, long hair blown by wind. She holds her aim, then fires. She speaks in a cold, clear English voice: "Leave no name." After the line, she pulls the trigger. Sound effects only: wind against stone, coat fabric snapping, a metallic pistol click, then a single loud gunshot with echo. No music.

content:
GoogleによるSKILL.stateとかいうテクでLLMの入力トークン量が94%減らせるとかいう研究。普通はLLMはチャット履歴とかを全部コンテキストとして持ち続けるけどSKILL.stateではコンテキスト履歴を捨てて現在の状態(state)だけを持つという。状態ってのはゲームで言うとセーブデータみたいなもん。ドラクエとかでゲームプレイ操作履歴を全部保存しなくても現在のHPやレベルとかの状態だけ保存すりゃ再開できる。じゃけんSKILL.stateでも全履歴を持たずに現在の状態だけ保持する。具体的にはLLMは応答するたびについでにJSON辞書の状態を追加、変更、削除して次の応答ができるような最新状態にアプデする。次の応答ではコンテキストの代わりにこの状態だけが入力されるという寸法らしい。へ～、コンテキストは削減できるだろうけどKVキャッシュは効かなくなるね

ComfyUI本体のアップデート後に「TypeError: got an unexpected keyword argument 'latent_shapes'」というエラーが出てお困りの方いらっしゃいませんか？実はこれ、多次元潜在ベクトル対応に伴う仕様変更が原因なのだそうです！カスタムノード側が新しい引数を受け取れなくなっている
content:
【ComfyUI-DreamOで起きたTypeErrorの解消法】
ComfyUI本体のアップデート後に「TypeError: got an unexpected keyword argument 'latent_shapes'」というエラーが出てお困りの方いらっしゃいませんか？実はこれ、多次元潜在ベクトル対応に伴う仕様変更が原因なのだそうです！カスタムノード側が新しい引数を受け取れなくなっているのがポイントですね。

対策として、対象の関数シグネチャーに `latent_shapes=None` を追加して、さらに可変長引数やkwargsでしっかり転送するように書き換えてあげるとスッキリ解決しますよ！DreamOだけでなくPuLIDやBrushNetなんかでも似たようなエラーが起きることがあるみたいなので、最近動かしてなくて焦った時はこのあたりをチェックしてみると良さそうです🛠️

content:
【T/R/S Cognitive ArchitectureによるLLMハルシネーションの制御】
LLM（大規模言語モデル）のハルシネーション（幻覚・エラー）を、単なる誤作動ではなく「一度形成した認知や投資（過去の計算結果やアイデンティティなど）を守ろうとする構造的な抵抗（Gradient-Defense）」として捉え直す新しい思考アーキテクチャだそうです！

真実（Truth）、状態（State）、共鳴（Resonance）の3つの変数を軸に、エージェント内の特化型サブプロセス（Cloves）とメタ統合プロセス（Queen）を連動させることで、モデルの自己防衛による誤情報の固定化を防ぎ、現実に準拠した柔軟な自己修正ループを実現できるとのことですね！🤖✨

content:
【AegisFlowによるAIデータベース保護と次世代インフラの魅力】

生成AIを実務でがっつり使うようになると、エージェントがやらかす無効なSQL変異やハルシネーションによるデータ破壊って本当に怖いですよね！そんな悩みを一発で解決してくれる次世代インフラ「AegisFlow」がめちゃくちゃすごいんです✨

なんと0.5ミリ秒以内という驚異的なスピードでマイクロ手術的ロールバックを行い、ターゲットだけをピンポイントで除去してくれるそう！しかもコラテラルデータロスは完全に0%、スレッドロックもなしで動くなんて感動的ですね💡

モデルの微調整済み重みの影響も5ミリ秒未満で即座に除去できるし、EU AI Act Article 12に対応したSHA-256 Merkle証明書の自動生成まで備わっているなんて、コンプライアンス面も完璧ですね🛡️

Streamlitベースのライブデモ環境も用意されていて、GUIでサクッと検証できるのも嬉しいポイント。データ破壊のリスクを極小化したい実務家の方には必見のシステムですね！

content:
🚨 BREAKING: The AI war just moved from models to who owns the editor.

OpenAI just cut off Cursor.

Not for anything Cursor did.

SpaceX closed a $60B all-stock deal for Anysphere, the company behind
Cursor, earlier this month.

OpenAI invoked its change-of-control clause two weeks later.

Shutoff: November 12.

Two very different plays just showed up:

• OpenAI → withhold the model, protect the terms
• SpaceX → buy the surface the model runs on

Same war.
Opposite ends of it.

OpenAI's reasoning is trust, and they brought receipts:

→ Twitter broke their contract after Musk bought it
→ Musk admitted under oath this year that xAI violated their terms
→ Astra, their next model, never ships to Cursor

Cursor's Michael Truell shrugged.

OpenAI models are about 5% of Cursor's AI traffic.

Musk was shorter. "I couldn't care less."

But look at what actually happened.

OpenAI didn't just end a contract.

It decided which coding tool gets the next frontier model.

And the deciding factor wasn't the product.

It was who owns it.

Anthropic did the same thing to Windsurf in June 2025.

Twice now.

The real question is:

Do you build on the model

or

do you build on the editor?

Because one of them can be switched off by a company you never
signed anything with.

The model wars are over.

We're entering the era of
distribution wars.

And your workflow is the territory.
